summary: Describes sixteen new TLS cipher suites using elliptic curve cryptography that specify stronger message authentication than the HMAC-SHA-1 used earlier. Eight use HMAC with SHA-256 or SHA-384, and eight use AES in Galois Counter Mode. They give TLS 1.2 users stronger options for elliptic-curve key exchange.

eli5.summary: It adds sixteen new combinations of locks and seals for secure web connections, so people who like small, fast elliptic-curve keys can pick stronger tamper-checking too.

subtitle: Sixteen TLS cipher suites that pair elliptic curve key exchange with SHA-256/384 and AES-GCM.

tldr.problem: The elliptic curve cipher suites for TLS in RFC 4492 all use HMAC-SHA1 as their MAC, and the IETF is gradually moving away from SHA-1 after recent analytic work on it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5289 defines 16 new cipher suites that keep the RFC 4492 elliptic curve key exchange and signatures. Eight use HMAC with SHA-256 or SHA-384, and eight use AES in Galois Counter Mode.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations get ECC cipher suites with stronger hashes and AEAD encryption, but the GCM suites may only be used with TLS 1.2 or greater. RFC 10015 updates this document.

today: RFC 5289 is updated by RFC 10015. The text of RFC 5289 itself says its security considerations rely on RFC 4346, RFC 4492 and RFC 5288, and that the suites may only be used with TLS 1.2 or greater.

sections.title: Why New ECC Cipher Suites
sections.content:
RFC 4492 describes Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) cipher suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS). All of them use HMAC-SHA1 as their Message Authentication Code (MAC) algorithm. Because of recent analytic work on SHA-1, the IETF is gradually moving away from SHA-1 and toward stronger hash algorithms.

This document specifies TLS ECC cipher suites that use SHA-256 and SHA-384 instead of SHA-1.

TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) also adds support for authenticated encryption with additional data (AEAD) cipher modes (RFC 5116). This document uses one such mode, Galois Counter Mode (GCM), for a second group of ECC suites. RFC 5288 covers GCM with other key establishment methods.
sections.eli5: The old locks used a seal that experts were starting to distrust. This document hands out new locks with stronger seals.

sections.title: Sixteen Suites in Two Families
sections.content:
The document defines 16 new cipher suites. All of them use Elliptic Curve Cryptography for key exchange and digital signature, as defined in RFC 4492. In other words, the key exchange and signature parts are unchanged; what changes is how data is protected and which hash is used.

The suites come in two groups of eight. The first group uses AES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode with an HMAC-based MAC. The second group uses AES in Galois Counter Mode. Within each group, the names show the key exchange (ECDHE or ECDH), the signature or certificate type (ECDSA or RSA), the AES key size (128 or 256) and the hash (SHA256 or SHA384).
sections.eli5: There are two boxes of eight locks each. One box uses a chain of linked blocks, the other uses a newer scrambling method.

sections.title: The HMAC-Based Suites
sections.content:
The first eight suites use AES in CBC mode with an HMAC-based MAC, for example TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256. They are the same as the corresponding RFC 4492 suites, whose names end in _SHA, except for the MAC and the Pseudo Random Function (PRF).

The RFC says these SHALL be as follows:

  • For suites ending _SHA256, the PRF is the TLS PRF with SHA-256 as the hash function, and the MAC is HMAC (RFC 2104) with SHA-256.
  • For suites ending _SHA384, the PRF is the TLS PRF with SHA-384 as the hash function, and the MAC is HMAC with SHA-384.
sections.eli5: These are the old locks with a better seal. The only changes are the stamp used to check nothing was tampered with and the recipe for mixing secret numbers.

sections.title: The Galois Counter Mode Suites
sections.content:
The second eight suites use the same asymmetric algorithms as the first group, but use the authenticated encryption modes defined in TLS 1.2, with AES in Galois Counter Mode (GCM). An example is TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.

These suites use the AEAD algorithms AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM described in RFC 5116, and GCM is used as described in RFC 5288.

Because AEAD handles integrity itself, only the PRF is specified: for suites ending _SHA256 it is the TLS PRF with SHA-256, and for suites ending _SHA384 it is the TLS PRF with SHA-384.
sections.eli5: Here the scrambling and the tamper check happen in one step, like a lock that also has the seal built in. The hash name only picks the recipe for mixing secret numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations in RFC 4346, RFC 4492 and RFC 5288 apply to this document as well. In addition, as described in RFC 5288, these cipher suites may only be used with TLS 1.2 or greater.
sections.eli5: The safety rules for the older locks still apply. These new locks also only work with the newest version of the secure connection.

sections.title: Assigned Cipher Suite Values
sections.content:
IANA has assigned a two-byte value to each of the 16 suites. The HMAC-based suites take values from {0xC0,0x23} to {0xC0,0x2A}, and the GCM-based suites take values from {0xC0,0x2B} to {0xC0,0x32}.

Within each group the order is ECDHE_ECDSA, ECDH_ECDSA, ECDHE_RSA, ECDH_RSA, and for each of these the 128-bit AES and SHA-256 suite comes first, followed by the 256-bit AES and SHA-384 suite.
sections.eli5: Each lock gets its own number so that both sides of a connection can say which one they want.
